blocks.text: But whatever these words may mean, a serious question is raised, namely, whether what is said here about locusts is to be explained literally. For many look for mysteries here, as though not real locusts were meant but the enemies of the Jews. Jerome seems to waver between the two opinions in such a way that he leans more towards the latter. For first he refers these things to the four empires which one after another rose up against the Jews. "The caterpillar," he says, "which in Hebrew is called גזם gazam, in Greek κάμπη [kampē], the Hebrews interpret as the Assyrians, the Babylonians and Chaldeans; who, coming from one region of the world, laid waste everything of the ten tribes as well as of the two, that is, of the Israelite people. The locust they interpret as the Medes and Persians; who, after overthrowing the empire of the Chaldeans, held the Jews captive. The bruchus as the Macedonians and all the successors of Alexander, and above all King Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who settled in Judaea like a bruchus and devoured all the remains left by the earlier kings. The blight they refer to the Roman empire; who, fourth and last, so oppressed the Jews as to drive them from their own territory." So he writes, as if from the mind of the Hebrews, who nevertheless, by his own admission, acknowledge that what is said here about locusts also happened literally. "The Jews," he says, "think that in the days of Joel so countless a multitude of locusts came upon Judaea that they filled everything; and left, I will not say the crops, but not even the bark and branches of the vines and trees." But he refutes this opinion of the Jews in what follows: "Whether this happened or not, we cannot clearly affirm. For the history of the Kings and Chronicles does not narrate it. And if it had happened, Scripture would certainly never have kept silent. We say only that under the metaphor of locusts the coming of enemies is described." Then, as if undecided between the two opinions: "If I am not mistaken," he says, "I seem to have found something in this Prophet. The impiety of the enemies is narrated under the figure of locusts. And again, the locusts themselves are spoken of as if they were compared to enemies: so that when you read of locusts you think of enemies; when you have thought of enemies, you return to the locusts." Cyril seems to agree with Jerome, understanding by these four plagues Shalmaneser, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus and the Romans. Yet in the same author you may read this: Ἀληθὲς μὲν οὖν τὸ χρῆμα, κἂν εἰ ἐπὶ ἀκρίδος τυχὸν νοοῖτο, βρούχου τε, καὶ κάμπης· [Alēthes men oun to chrēma, kan ei epi akridos tychon nooito, brouchou te, kai kampēs] "This is indeed true, even if it be taken of the locust, the bruchus and the caterpillar." Theodoret, after writing that some interpret these things figuratively of four kings of Assyria, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar, says: Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀληθῆ μὲν ἡγοῦμαι καὶ ταῦτα· ὑπολαμβάνω δὲ καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν νοούμενα τῷ ὄντι γεγενῆσθαι· [Egō de alēthē men hēgoumai kai tauta; hypolambanō de kai ta kata to rhēton nooumena tō onti gegenēsthai] "I indeed consider these things true; [III, 292] but I also think that what is understood literally really happened." The Chaldee mostly embraces the literal sense. Sometimes, however, he slips into the mystical: as in Ioel. II, 25., where for the four kinds of locusts, arbe, jelek, chasil and gazam, he has עממיא ולשניא ושלטוניא ומלכותא פרענות, "peoples, and tongues, and dominions, and kingdoms of vengeance"; that is, those whom God used to take vengeance on the rebels among his people. Of the Hebrew commentators, Jarchi, Kimchi and Aben Ezra cling tenaciously to the letter. But Abarbanel, later than these, following Jerome, [col. 467] asserts that this Prophet came להתנבאות על ממשלת ארבע המלכיות בבל ופרס ויון ורומי, "to prophesy concerning the dominion of the four empires, namely the Babylonian, and the Persian, and the Greek, and the Roman." And he is so averse to the literal sense that, dealing with those who refer these things to locusts, he exclaims in the very preface: חלילה לי מלהאמין בזה, "Far be it from me to believe this", as though it were utterly absurd. But since he objects nothing that is not most futile, I do not doubt that real locusts are meant by the Prophet, which laid waste Judaea shortly after his prophecy. For hostile enemies are not usually compared with locusts except in respect of number: as when it is said of the Midianites and Amalekites, Iud. VI, 5., "They came like locusts in multitude." And Iud. VII, 12., "They were spread out in that valley like locusts in multitude." And Iudith. II, 2., of the forces of the Assyrians: "And many of mixed stock, like locusts, gathered to them." And of the Trojans and the Ethiopians whom Memnon had brought, Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 2, line 195.
